lessons.briefing:
When cellular base stations lose grid power or fiber backhauls are severed, electromagnetic
radio waves remain the only medium that travels freely across terrain with zero physical
infrastructure. However, connecting a transmitter to an improper antenna converts costly
radio energy into destructive heat that incinerates the transmitter’s final output transistors.
This day decodes radio spectrum bands (HF, VHF, UHF), electromagnetic wavelength physics,
resonant antenna element calculations (quarter-wave ground plane and half-wave dipole),
coaxial impedance matching (50 Ω), and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) measurement.
lessons.briefingSw:
Minara ya simu inapopoteza umeme au nyaya za fiber kukatika, mawimbi ya redio
ndiyo njia pekee ya kuwasiliana bila miundombinu. Lakini ukiunganisha redio kwenye
antena isiyo sahihi, nguvu ya redio inarudi nyuma na kuchoma transistor za redio.
Siku hii inafundisha jinsi ya kukokotoa urefu wa antena na kupima SWR.
lessons.contentMd:
## The Electromagnetic Spectrum for Resilient Communications

Radio waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields traveling at the speed of light ($c \approx 300,000\text{ km/s}$).

| Band | Frequency Range | Typical Propagation | Primary Emergency Application |
|------|-----------------|---------------------|-------------------------------|
| **HF (High Frequency)** | 3 – 30 MHz | Ground wave + Ionospheric skywave refraction | Long-range (100–3,000 km) regional communication without repeaters |
| **VHF (Very High Frequency)** | 30 – 300 MHz | Line-of-sight + diffraction over ridges | Local community tactical comms (5–35 km); marine & aviation |
| **UHF (Ultra High Frequency)** | 300 – 3,000 MHz | Strict line-of-sight; penetrates buildings | Urban handhelds, LoRa packet mesh networks, and repeater links |

## The Wavelength Equation & Antenna Lengths

The fundamental speed-of-light relationship determines how long an antenna must be to resonate with a given radio frequency:

$$\lambda\text{ (meters)} = \frac{300}{f\text{ (MHz)}}$$

Because radio waves travel ~5% slower through copper/aluminum wire than in free vacuum (velocity factor $k \approx 0.95$), the practical formula for a **Half-Wave Dipole Antenna ($\lambda / 2$)** is:

$$L\text{ (meters)} = \frac{142.5}{f\text{ (MHz)}}$$

### Worked Example: 2-Meter Emergency VHF Band (145.000 MHz)
$$L = \frac{142.5}{145.0} = 0.9828\text{ meters (98.3 cm total dipole length)}$$
Each quarter-wave leg of the dipole = $98.3 \div 2 = \mathbf{49.1\text{ cm}}$.

## The 1/4-Wave Ground Plane Antenna (Field Build)

The most durable, omni-directional field antenna can be constructed from an SO-239 chassis connector and five pieces of stiff copper wire:
1. **Vertical radiator ($\lambda / 4$):** Solder a stiff copper rod ($49.1\text{ cm}$ for 145 MHz) into the center pin of the connector.
2. **Radials ($\lambda / 4$):** Bolt four identical wire lengths ($51.5\text{ cm}$, cut 5% longer) through the four mounting holes on the connector flange.
3. **Angle of droop:** Bend the four radials downward at **45 degrees**. Bending the radials down from horizontal raises the feedpoint impedance from $35\text{ }\Omega$ to exactly **$50\text{ }\Omega$**, creating a perfect match for standard coaxial cables!

## Characteristic Impedance & Standing Wave Ratio (SWR)

Transceivers, coaxial cables, and antennas are engineered for a standard **$50\text{ }\Omega$ (Ohm) impedance**.

When an antenna’s impedance does not match the $50\text{ }\Omega$ cable:
- Part of the transmitted RF power is radiated into the air (**Forward Power**).
- The remaining power bounces off the antenna and travels back down the cable toward the radio (**Reflected Power**).
- The interference between forward and reflected waves creates standing voltage nodes, quantified as **Standing Wave Ratio (SWR)**.

| SWR Value | Reflected Power (%) | Condition & Action |
|-----------|---------------------|--------------------|
| **1.0 : 1** | **0.0%** | **Perfect theoretical resonance**; 100% of RF power is radiated |
| **1.1 – 1.5 : 1** | **< 4.0%** | **Excellent operational range**; safe for continuous transmission |
| **1.6 – 2.0 : 1** | **4.0% – 11.1%** | **Acceptable in emergencies**; minor range loss |
| **2.1 – 3.0 : 1** | **11.1% – 25.0%** | **Poor**; radio will run hot; foldback protection will throttle power |
| **> 3.0 : 1** | **> 25.0%** | **DANGER**: High reflected voltage will destroy final amplifier transistors! |

## The 50 Ω Dummy Load

Never tune or test a transmitter on live frequencies without an antenna or dummy load. Transmitting into an open cable (SWR $\infty:1$) creates massive reflected voltage peaks that puncture the dielectric gates of RF power MOSFETs in milliseconds.
- A **dummy load** consists of a non-inductive $50\text{ }\Omega$ power resistor enclosed in a shielded can. It absorbs RF energy and converts it harmlessly into heat without radiating interference into community airwaves.

exercises.explanation:
Correct! An SWR of 3.8:1 reflects over 34% of your power directly back into the radio's sensitive power amplifier. Prolonged transmission under this mismatch will burn out the final transistors. Unkey and check antenna length and cable continuity.

Why the other options are wrong: Increasing power will quadruple the reflected voltage, instantly destroying the final output transistors. Battery level has no relation to RF impedance matching or transistor heat dissipation. SWR is a property of the antenna geometry and frequency, independent of modulation mode.

options.text: Increase transmitter power to 100W to force the signal past the antenna resistance
Continue talking as long as the battery indicator shows green
Release the transmit key immediately; inspect the antenna elements for incorrect length, short circuits, or broken coaxial connections
Switch from FM mode to AM mode to bypass the SWR reading

exercises.prompt: You connect an SWR meter between a 50W VHF transceiver and an improvised antenna. The meter reads an SWR of 3.8:1 when keyed. What should you do immediately?

exercises.explanation: 142.5 / 142.5 = 1.0 meter total wire length (each quarter-wave leg will be 0.50 meters or 50 cm long).
exercises.prompt: Using the formula L = 142.5 / f(MHz), the total physical length of a half-wave dipole wire antenna for the 142.5 MHz frequency is exactly ___ meter(s).

right.text: Refracts off the ionosphere to provide regional communications over 100–1000+ km
Reliable line-of-sight communication over 10–50 km with compact antennas
Superior penetration through urban concrete walls and dense forest foliage
Absorbs transmitted RF power as heat for safe transmitter calibration

exercises.prompt: Match each radio frequency band to its operational characteristic.

lessons.outline:
1. The electromagnetic spectrum: HF (3–30 MHz), VHF (30–300 MHz), and UHF (300–3000 MHz)
2. Wavelength equation: Relating frequency to physical physical antenna size (λ = 300 / f)
3. The Half-Wave Dipole: Physical length formula (L = 142.5 / f) and center radiation resistance
4. The 1/4-Wave Ground Plane antenna: Vertical radiator with four 45-degree droop radials
5. Characteristic impedance: Why RF transmission lines are standardized at 50 Ohms
6. Standing Wave Ratio (SWR): Forward power vs reflected power (safe operating thresholds)
7. High SWR hazards: Thermal destruction of output RF final transistors (MOSFETs)
8. Antenna tuning & dummy loads: 50 Ω non-inductive resistor testing before live transmission

lessons.briefing:
Dual-band VHF/UHF handheld transceivers (such as the Baofeng UV-5R and UV-82 series)
cost under KSh 4,000 in Nairobi and are ubiquitous among community patrols, wildlife
rangers, and agricultural cooperatives. However, improper configuration (wrong squelch,
misconfigured repeater offsets, or inadvertent CTCSS blocking) renders them useless
during crises. This day teaches transceiver architecture, simplex direct vs repeater
duplex operation, CTCSS/DCS sub-audible tones, standard international radio etiquette
(ICAO phonetic alphabet), distress protocols (MAYDAY vs PAN-PAN), and power management.
lessons.briefingSw:
Redio za mkono za VHF/UHF (kama Baofeng UV-5R) zinapatikana kwa bei nafuu Nairobi na
zinatumika sana na walinzi na wakulima. Lakini bila kuelewa jinsi ya kurekebisha squelch,
repeater offsets, na CTCSS tones, mawasiliano ya dharura yatakwama. Siku hii inafundisha
uendeshaji sahihi, kanuni za simu za dharura (MAYDAY na PAN-PAN), na kutumia sauti ya ICAO.
lessons.contentMd:
## Transceiver Architecture & Key Controls

Common handhelds (e.g. Baofeng UV-5R, TYT, Quansheng) operate across two primary bands:
- **VHF (136 – 174 MHz):** Exceptional range in rural, open terrain and water.
- **UHF (400 – 480 MHz):** Shorter wavelength (~70 cm); penetrates concrete buildings and dense forest canopies.

### Critical Knobs and Menu Settings:
- **Power / Volume Knob:** Rotary switch on top.
- **PTT (Push-To-Talk):** Large rubber side switch. Press firmly to transmit; release to receive.
- **SQL (Squelch Level, Menu 0):** Sets the background noise threshold.
  - Set to **Level 2 or 3**: Mutes ambient atmospheric static while remaining sensitive to distant signals.
  - Setting to Level 8 or 9 requires an overwhelmingly strong signal to open the audio gate, deafening your radio to weak emergency transmissions!
- **TXP (Transmit Power, Menu 2):**
  - **LOW (1 Watt):** Extends battery life by 400%; sufficient for line-of-sight comms up to 3 km.
  - **HIGH (4–8 Watts):** Use only when communicating through obstacles or over long distances.

## Simplex vs Repeater Duplex Operation

### 1. Simplex Operation (Direct Radio-to-Radio)
Both transceivers transmit and receive on the exact same frequency.
- Example: Unit A and Unit B both set to `145.500 MHz`.
- Simple, requires zero infrastructure, but range is limited by terrain and curvature of the Earth (typically 3–15 km from ground level).

### 2. Duplex Repeater Operation (Overcoming Mountains & Distance)
A **repeater** is a high-power transceiver mounted on an elevated tower or mountain ridge (e.g. Ngong Hills, Mount Longonot). It listens on one frequency (**Input**) and instantaneously re-broadcasts on another frequency (**Output**) with 50–100 Watts:
- **Standard 2-Meter VHF Offset:** $\pm 600\text{ kHz (0.6 MHz)}$.
- **Standard 70-Centimeter UHF Offset:** $\pm 5.0\text{ MHz}$.

### CTCSS / DCS Tones (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch)
Repeaters and community nets often require a sub-audible tone (e.g. `100.0 Hz` CTCSS) transmitted alongside your voice to open their receiver:
- **Tone does NOT encrypt your transmission.** Anyone on the frequency can still hear you.
- If you transmit without the correct tone, the repeater ignores your transmission.
- In community simplex nets, setting receive CTCSS blocks interference from neighboring users.

## International Radio Etiquette & Discipline

In emergencies, panicked rambling blocks frequencies. Communications must be crisp and standardized:

### The Golden PTT Rule:
> **Think before you key.** Press PTT $\rightarrow$ Wait **1 full second** (allows tone and repeater carrier to settle) $\rightarrow$ Speak clearly across the microphone (not directly into it) $\rightarrow$ Release PTT immediately.

### Standard Prowords:
| Proword | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| **ROGER** | "I have received and understood your last transmission." |
| **SAY AGAIN** | "Repeat your last transmission." (Never say 'repeat' — 'repeat' means artillery barrage in military doctrine!) |
| **AFFIRMATIVE / NEGATIVE** | "Yes" / "No" (clearer over noisy channels) |
| **STANDBY** | "Acknowledge call; pause for more info." |
| **OVER** | "I have finished speaking; response expected." |
| **OUT** | "Conversation ended; channel clear." (Never say 'Over and Out' together!) |

### Emergency Distress Calls:
- **MAYDAY (Repeated 3 times):** Immediate life-or-death emergency (sinking boat, catastrophic bleed, armed attack). Clears all non-essential traffic immediately.
- **PAN-PAN (Repeated 3 times):** Urgent situation concerning safety of a person or vehicle (broken vehicle in wilderness, severe injury with stable vitals).
- **SECURITE (Repeated 3 times):** Safety bulletin (approaching flash flood, fallen high-voltage power lines).

exercises.explanation:
Correct! With a -600 kHz (-0.600 MHz) offset, your radio listens on the repeater's output (145.600 MHz) and shifts down to transmit on the repeater's input: 145.600 - 0.600 = 145.000 MHz.

Why the other options are wrong: Transmitting on the same frequency is simplex; repeaters operate duplex on different transmit and receive frequencies. 146.200 MHz would be a positive (+0.600 MHz) offset, not a negative offset. This jumps to a completely different band (UHF instead of VHF).

options.text: 145.600 MHz (same frequency)

exercises.prompt: You are attempting to reach a mountain repeater with an output frequency of 145.600 MHz and a standard negative offset of 600 kHz (-0.6 MHz). What frequency should your radio transmit on when you press the PTT button?

exercises.explanation: MAYDAY (from the French 'venez m'aider' - come help me) is the universal distress signal. It halts all other radio traffic on the channel to prioritize the emergency casualty or craft.
exercises.prompt: The highest-priority international radio distress call, used strictly when life is in immediate, grave danger, is spoken as the word ___ repeated three times.

right.text: Silences continuous background static while allowing weak signals to open speaker
Inaudible low-frequency audio tone required to open repeater receiver gates
Preserves 80% battery capacity during short-range line-of-sight communication

lessons.outline:
1. Handheld transceiver architecture: Antenna port (SMA), PTT button, volume/power, squelch
2. Simplex communication: Direct radio-to-radio on a single shared frequency
3. Repeater Duplex operation: Transmit offsets (+/- 600 kHz on 2m VHF; +/- 5.0 MHz on 70cm UHF)
4. Squelch mechanisms: Carrier squelch threshold vs CTCSS/DCS sub-audible tone decoders
5. The PTT (Push-To-Talk) technique: Press, pause one second, speak across the mic, release
6. Emergency message traffic: MAYDAY (life distress) vs PAN-PAN (urgency) vs SECURITE (safety)

lessons.briefing:
In rugged East African topographies — spanning the Rift Valley escarpment, Mount Kenya,
and the Aberdare ranges — line-of-sight VHF/UHF signals cannot penetrate high volcanic
ridges. Standard long-range HF radio fires waves at shallow angles, creating a deadly
"skip zone" where signals bounce 1,000 km away, leaving the critical 50 to 400 km regional
zone completely deaf. Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) overcomes this by firing
radio waves nearly straight up (70°–90°) into the ionospheric F-layer, reflecting them
straight down like an umbrella to blanket deep valleys and mountain passes. This day
teaches ionospheric refraction layers, NVIS antenna design, and Continuous Wave (CW).
lessons.briefingSw:
Kwenye milima na mabonde kama Bonde la Ufa na Mlima Kenya, redio za kawaida za VHF/UHF
haziwezi kupita milimani. Teknolojia ya NVIS (Near Vertical Incidence Skywave) hurusha
mawimbi ya HF moja kwa moja angani (nyuzi 70-90) yakigonga ionosphere na kurudi chini
kufunika eneo lote la kilomita 50 hadi 400 bila kizuizi cha milima.
lessons.contentMd:
## The Ionosphere & The Skip Zone Dilemma

The upper atmosphere (60 to 400 km above Earth) is ionized by solar ultraviolet radiation into distinct layers:
- **D-Layer (60–90 km):** Present only in daytime; absorbs lower HF frequencies (below 5 MHz). Disappears at dusk.
- **E-Layer (90–150 km):** Moderately ionized; supports medium-range hops.
- **F-Layer (150–400 km):** Splits into F1 and F2 by day, combines at night. **The primary mirror for long-range HF skywaves.**

### The Disaster of the "Skip Zone":
Standard HF antennas fire waves at low angles (10°–30°) toward the horizon.
- The **ground wave** dies out after 20–40 km due to soil attenuation.
- The **skywave** hits the ionosphere at a shallow angle and reflects back down at 800–2,000 km.
- The area between 40 km and 800 km is the **Skip Zone (Dead Zone)** — complete silence! If an earthquake or flood occurs in Nakuru or Nyeri, a low-angle HF station in Nairobi cannot reach them.

## Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS)

NVIS solves the skip zone by altering antenna geometry to direct radiation **straight up (70° to 90° above horizontal)**:
- The radio energy strikes the F-layer almost perpendicular to the ionospheric boundary.
- As long as the frequency is below the **Critical Frequency ($f_o\text{F2}$)**, the wave refracts directly downward, blanketing a circular area from **0 to 400 km radius** without any dead zones.
- Volcanic mountain ranges, deep canyons, and heavy forest canopies are completely irrelevant — the signal arrives from straight above!

### Operating Frequency Rules (East Africa):
- **Daytime (high solar ionization):** Use **7.0 – 7.3 MHz (40-meter band)**. D-layer absorption is overcome; $f_o\text{F2}$ is high.
- **Nighttime (ionization drops, D-layer vanishes):** Drop down to **3.5 – 3.8 MHz (80-meter band)**.

## The Low-Slung NVIS Dipole (Field Build)

Standard wisdom says an antenna must be elevated as high as possible. **NVIS requires the exact opposite!**

1. **Antenna Height:** Hang a half-wave dipole only **0.1 to 0.2 wavelengths above ground**:
   - On 40 meters (7.1 MHz): $\lambda = 42\text{ m} \rightarrow$ Height = **3 to 4 meters off the ground** (suspended on tree branches or bamboo).
   - At this low height, the earth beneath the antenna acts as an RF reflector, focusing the radiation pattern straight upward into the sky.
2. **Ground Reflector Wire (Gain Booster):**
   - Lay a single bare wire along the ground directly beneath the suspended dipole, cut 5% longer than the antenna.
   - The earth reflector directs an additional 3 dB of RF power straight up into the ionosphere.

## Continuous Wave (CW / Morse Code)

When solar storms disrupt the ionosphere or transmitter battery reserves drop to 5 Watts, voice (SSB) communication fails. **CW (Continuous Wave / Morse Code) remains audible when all voice is unreadable.**

### Why CW Outperforms Voice:
- **Bandwidth:** SSB voice requires **2,800 Hz** of receiver bandwidth. CW requires only **100 Hz**.
- **Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR):** Concentrating 5 Watts into a 100 Hz bandwidth delivers an effective **14 dB gain** over voice — equivalent to a 25-fold increase in transmitter power!
- A human ear can decode a pure audio tone buried deep beneath background static.

### Universal Emergency Morse Signal:
$$\mathbf{S\text{ (}\cdot\cdot\cdot\text{) }\quad O\text{ (---) }\quad S\text{ (}\cdot\cdot\cdot\text{)}}$$
- 3 short dits (units of 1)
- 3 long dahs (each equal to 3 dits)
- 3 short dits
- Standard pause between letters = 3 dits; between words = 7 dits.

exercises.explanation:
Correct! Placing a horizontal dipole 0.1 to 0.2 wavelengths above ground uses ground reflection to cancel low-angle horizon radiation and direct almost all RF energy upward into the ionospheric F-layer.

Why the other options are wrong: While lower antennas have lower strike probability, that is not the RF engineering reason. NVIS is a skywave mode that travels through the ionosphere, not a surface ground wave. Tower height does not affect the voltage requirements of a transmitter.

options.text: To protect the antenna wire from lightning strikes
Because low frequencies travel faster along the surface of moist soil
The proximity of the conductive earth acts as a ground reflector, beaming the radio waves straight up into the ionosphere at steep 70-90 degree angles
Handheld transceivers cannot supply enough voltage to pump signals up a tall tower

exercises.prompt: Why must a Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) dipole antenna be hung close to the ground (only 2 to 4 meters high) rather than mounted atop a high tower?

exercises.explanation: The 40-meter band (7.0 to 7.3 MHz) is the universal daytime NVIS band in equatorial regions. At night, as ionospheric electron density drops, operators switch to the 80-meter band (3.5 to 3.8 MHz).
exercises.prompt: During daytime in East Africa, the primary NVIS frequency band used to communicate regionally over 0 to 400 km is the ___ meter band (around 7 MHz).

right.text: The silent gap between the end of the ground wave and the first skywave return
The highest frequency that reflects back down when sent vertically into the ionosphere
Ultra-narrow 100 Hz transmission mode with a 14 dB signal-to-noise advantage over voice
Wire laid on the earth below an NVIS dipole to boost upward radiation by 3 dB

exercises.prompt: Match each long-range radio concept to its definition.

lessons.outline:
1. The ionospheric layers: D-layer (daytime absorption), E-layer, and F1/F2 refracting layers
2. The Skip Zone dilemma: Ground wave fading at 30 km while skywave lands at 800 km
3. The NVIS principle: High-angle radiation (70°–90°) reflecting downwards like an umbrella
4. NVIS frequency window: Critical frequency (foF2) — 80m (3.5–4.0 MHz) night, 40m (7.0–7.3 MHz) day
5. The Low-Slung Dipole: Erecting a horizontal wire only 2 to 4 meters above ground
6. Ground reflector wire: Enhancing upward signal reflection by 3 dB
7. Continuous Wave (CW / Morse Code): 100 Hz bandwidth advantage over 2.8 kHz SSB voice
8. International distress Morse: S-O-S (... --- ...) transmission mechanics and tone recognition

lessons.briefing:
When cellular towers go dark and mobile data networks collapse, modern low-cost digital
packet radio can maintain encrypted community messaging, GPS distress beacons, and sensor
telemetry across entire counties without internet or subscriptions. LoRa (Long Range)
uses Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation to decode digital packets buried 20 dB below the
ambient noise floor. Running open-source Meshtastic firmware on low-power battery nodes
(costing under KSh 3,500), each device automatically routes and repeats encrypted packets
from peer to peer. This day covers LoRa modulation, mesh routing protocols, AES-256
encryption, solar-powered hilltop repeater nodes, and field telemetry bridges.
lessons.briefingSw:
Minara ya Safaricom au Airtel ikizimika, teknolojia ya LoRa (Long Range) na Meshtastic
inaruhusu kutuma ujumbe wa maandishi, mahali ulipo (GPS), na taarifa za dharura kwa
simu za kawaida kupitia Bluetooth bila intaneti, bila vocha, na bila minara ya simu.
Kila kifaa kidogo cha KSh 3,000 kinajenga mtandao wa bure unaorudia mawimbi.
lessons.contentMd:
## What is LoRa & Chirp Spread Spectrum?

Conventional radio modems send data on a fixed frequency. High noise or interference drowns them out.
**LoRa (Long Range)** modulates digital bits using **Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS)**:
- The signal frequency continuously sweeps (chirps) up or down across a bandwidth (e.g. 125 kHz or 250 kHz).
- The receiver uses mathematical correlation to lock onto the chirp pattern even when the signal power is **20 dB weaker than the background thermal noise floor**!
- Transmit power of only **100 milliwatts (0.1 W)** regularly achieves **15 to 40+ km line-of-sight**.

### Frequency Bands for East Africa (ITU Region 1):
- **433 MHz Band:** Excellent tree canopy and terrain penetration; shared with amateur radio and car remotes.
- **868 MHz Band:** Standard European/African license-exempt Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) band. Max allowable ERP: 25–500 mW.

## The Meshtastic Decentralized Mesh Architecture

Unlike cellular networks that depend on central towers:
- In a **Meshtastic mesh**, every single node is both a client and a **packet repeater**.
- When Node A sends an encrypted message to Node D (out of direct range), Node B and Node C automatically receive the packet, verify its packet ID has not been seen before, and re-transmit it with a decremented **Hop Limit** (typically 3–5 hops max).
- If a relay node is destroyed, packets automatically find alternative routes through other community members’ nodes.

### Node Roles:
- **CLIENT:** The normal portable node. Connects via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to an Android or iPhone running the free Meshtastic app. You type SMS-style messages on your phone; the LoRa radio transmits them over the air.
- **ROUTER / REPEATER:** A dedicated, permanently mounted node placed on a tall tree, water tank, or mountain summit. It does not connect to a phone; its sole purpose is to listen 24/7 and re-transmit packets with prioritized antenna elevation.

## Security: AES-256 Encryption

Community radio is traditionally open to eavesdropping. Meshtastic solves this with military-grade cryptography:
- **Public Channel (Default):** Uses a well-known default key (`AQ==`). Used for disaster distress beacons, weather alerts, and coordinating with arriving relief workers.
- **Private Channels:** Encrypted using a randomly generated **AES-256-bit symmetric key**.
- A 256-bit key shared via QR code allows community leaders, medical clinics, or security patrols to communicate across the shared mesh with complete privacy. Unauthenticated third parties see only scrambled pseudo-random noise packets.

## Building an Autonomous Solar Mountain Node

A single solar-powered LoRa relay placed atop an escarpment or water tower can link an entire rural district:

### Hardware Components:
1. **Radio Module:** RAK Wireless WisBlock (nRF52840 + SX1262 LoRa). Consumes only **15 microamps ($\mu\text{A}$)** in deep sleep — 100× more efficient than ESP32 boards!
2. **Energy Storage:** Two Panasonic 18650 Li-ion cells (3,400 mAh each in parallel = 6,800 mAh at 3.7V). Provides **14 days of continuous operation in complete darkness**.
3. **Solar Harvest:** 5 Watt, 6 Volt monocrystalline solar panel with an onboard solar MPPT charge controller.
4. **Antenna:** High-gain fiberglass collinear antenna (3 dBi to 5.8 dBi) mounted vertically at the top of a bamboo or PVC conduit mast.
5. **Weatherproof Housing:** IP67 polycarbonate electrical junction box with silicone cable glands.

exercises.explanation:
Correct! Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation provides substantial processing gain. The receiver correlates known frequency chirps out of thermal noise, enabling decoding at negative Signal-to-Noise Ratios (-20 dB SNR) that would completely garble standard FM or AM voice.

Why the other options are wrong: LoRa is a peer-to-peer terrestrial packet radio system completely independent of satellites. LoRa uses fractions of a watt (0.1W) and does not emit high microwave voltages. LoRa transmits electromagnetic radio waves, not mechanical acoustic sound waves.

options.text: It uses satellite cellular uplinks provided by Starlink
It pulses extremely high microwave voltages that burn through foliage
It converts radio waves into ultrasonic sound waves
It sweeps carrier frequency across a wide bandwidth, allowing mathematical correlators to decode packets even when signal strength is 20 dB below background noise

exercises.prompt: How does LoRa Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) modulation achieve reliable communication over 30+ km with only 100 milliwatts of transmit power?

exercises.explanation: Meshtastic supports AES-256 bit symmetric key encryption. Sharing the encryption key securely (via offline QR code or secure transfer) allows private group communications that cannot be read by other mesh participants.
exercises.prompt: Meshtastic private group channels are encrypted using the industry-standard ___ symmetric encryption cipher to prevent unauthorized eavesdropping on the open airwaves.

right.text: Handheld radio connected via Bluetooth to a smartphone for text messaging
Autonomous solar-powered radio on a high vantage point to relay packets
Prevents packets from bouncing indefinitely in infinite loops across the mesh

lessons.outline:
1. The LoRa revolution: Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) and decoding signals below noise floor (-20 dB)
2. Frequency allocation in Kenya: 433 MHz and 868 MHz ISM bands (license-exempt power limits)
3. The Meshtastic protocol: Decentralized flooding and managed mesh routing (zero internet required)
4. Node roles: Client (handheld with smartphone app), Router (permanent high-elevation relay)
5. Cryptographic security: AES-256 pre-shared keys for private channels and unencrypted broadcast nets
6. Hardware architectures: ESP32 + SX1262 (Heltec V3) vs Ultra-low-power nRF52 (RAK4631)
7. Solar repeater engineering: 5W solar panel + TP4056 charge controller + dual 18650 Li-ion cells
8. Offline data integration: Bridging LoRa text packets to offline local campus servers (Kiwix / PWA)

lessons.briefing:
In radio communications, antenna elevation is power: elevating an antenna from 2 meters
to 10 meters above ground quadruples your operational VHF line-of-sight range. However,
erecting an elevated metal mast in thunderstorm-prone regions of East Africa (such as
the Lake Victoria basin, which experiences over 200 thunderstorm days annually) creates
an enormous lightning strike hazard. Connecting an ungrounded mast to indoor radio equipment
invites catastrophic fire, equipment destruction, and fatal electric shock. This final
day covers radio horizon trigonometry, guyed mast engineering (bamboo and conduit),
coaxial cable attenuation physics, and single-point RF lightning grounding standards.

lessons.contentMd:
## The Radio Horizon & Elevation Mathematics

Because the Earth is a curved sphere, line-of-sight radio waves travel until they meet the optical horizon. Refraction slightly bends VHF/UHF waves around the curvature (effective Earth radius factor $k = 4/3$).

### The Radio Line-of-Sight Formula:
$$D\text{ (km)} = 3.57 \times \left(\sqrt{h_1} + \sqrt{h_2}\right)$$
Where:
- $h_1$ = Height of transmitter antenna (meters)
- $h_2$ = Height of receiver antenna (meters)

### The Math in Practice:
- Two operators holding Baofeng radios at head height ($h = 1.7\text{ m}$):
  $$D = 3.57 \times (\sqrt{1.7} + \sqrt{1.7}) = 3.57 \times (1.30 + 1.30) = \mathbf{9.3\text{ km maximum flat horizon range}}$$
- Operator A climbs a hill or raises their antenna to **10 meters** ($h_1 = 10\text{ m}$):
  $$D = 3.57 \times (\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{1.7}) = 3.57 \times (3.16 + 1.30) = \mathbf{15.9\text{ km}}$$
**Elevation delivers more practical range than quadrupling transmitter wattage!**

## Guyed Mast Engineering: 3-Way Triangulation

To support a 6 to 12-meter mast built from treated bamboo poles or interlocking galvanized EMT electrical conduit:
1. **Base Plate:** Rest the mast base on a flat paving stone or concrete block with a locating pin. Never bury a wooden/bamboo mast directly in dirt (it will rot at the soil line within 12 months).
2. **Guy Triangulation at 120 Degrees:**
   - Anchor points must be spaced symmetrically at **120 degrees** around the mast.
   - The anchor distance from the base should equal **at least 60% of the mast height** (e.g. for a 10m mast, anchors are placed 6m out).
3. **Guy Materials:** UV-resistant Dacron cord or galvanized 3 mm steel wire with turnbuckles.
4. **Ground Anchors:** Steel earth screws driven at a 45-degree angle pointing away from the mast.

## Coaxial Cable Selection: Don’t Waste Power

Cheap, thin coaxial cable (*RG-58*) has high internal resistance at VHF and UHF frequencies:

| Cable Type | Diameter | Loss per 30m @ 145 MHz (VHF) | Loss per 30m @ 433 MHz (UHF) | Recommendation |
|------------|----------|------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------|
| **RG-58** | 5.0 mm | **4.8 dB (67% power lost!)** | **9.2 dB (88% power lost!)** | Portable runs < 5 meters only |
| **RG-213** | 10.3 mm | **2.2 dB (40% power lost)** | **4.2 dB (62% power lost)** | Good general-purpose base station |
| **LMR-400** | 10.3 mm | **1.5 dB (29% power lost)** | **2.7 dB (46% power lost)** | **Best**: Mandatory for UHF & long runs |

*A 3 dB loss halves your transmitted power.* Running 30 meters of RG-58 on UHF turns a 5-Watt radio transmission into only **0.6 Watts** at the antenna!

## Lightning Protection & RF Grounding

The highlands of Kenya, Uganda, and the Lake Victoria basin experience some of the highest lightning flash densities on the planet (over 50 strikes/km²/year).

### The 4 Golden Rules of Lightning Protection:
1. **Gas Discharge Tube Surge Arrestor:**
   - Install a 50 $\Omega$ coaxial surge protector (e.g. PolyPhaser or Diamond SP3000) at the building entrance point **before** the cable enters living quarters.
2. **Short, Straight Downlead:**
   - Connect the surge protector and metal mast to the earth electrode using heavy **16 mm² bare copper conductor**.
   - **Avoid sharp 90-degree bends!** High-frequency lightning surge pulses have massive inductive impedance; they will arc straight off sharp wire bends through walls and into electrical wiring.
3. **Deep Earth Electrode:**
   - Drive a **2.4-meter (8-foot) copper-clad steel earth rod** fully into moist ground.
   - If soil is rocky or dry sand, dig a horizontal trench and bed the rod in bentonite clay or charcoal and agricultural salt to lower ground resistance below $10\text{ }\Omega$.
4. **The "Ugly Balun" (RF Choke):**
   - Wind 6 turns of your coaxial feedline around a 10 cm PVC pipe directly below the antenna feedpoint.
   - Stops RF currents from flowing back down the outside shield of the cable into the radio room.

exercises.explanation:
Correct! High-frequency UHF signals (433 MHz) suffer massive dielectric and resistive losses in thin cables. A 9.2 dB loss leaves less than 12% of transmitter power reaching the antenna. High-grade low-loss cable (like LMR-400 or RG-213) must be used for UHF runs exceeding 5 meters.

Why the other options are wrong: There is no indication of physical lightning damage. All radio frequencies travel through properly rated coaxial transmission lines. Earth's magnetic field does not attenuate RF signals inside coaxial cables.

options.text: The radio was struck by lightning during installation
UHF radio waves cannot travel through coaxial cables
The earth's magnetic field cancels out vertical cable runs
RG-58 cable suffers extreme attenuation (~9.2 dB loss per 30m at 433 MHz), which dissipates over 88% of the radio's power as heat before it reaches the antenna

exercises.prompt: An operator connects a 433 MHz LoRa transceiver to an antenna mounted on a 30-meter tall mast using thin RG-58 coaxial cable. Testing shows almost no signal reaching the next node. Why?

exercises.explanation: Lightning discharges contain high-frequency impulse currents where sharp bends create high inductive reactance. The lightning surge will jump (side-flash) directly off a sharp 90-degree corner rather than following the wire into the ground rod.
exercises.prompt: When installing a heavy copper lightning downlead conductor from an antenna mast to the ground rod, you must avoid sharp ___ degree bends because high-frequency lightning energy will arc off the corner.
Practical Assessment: Document your field antenna construction, coaxial connection, or RF lightning grounding installation.

rubric.criterion: Antenna element or ground system constructed according to engineering specifications (dipole, ground plane, or mast grounding downlead)
Coaxial connector (SO-239, BNC, SMA, or PL-259) soldered or crimped cleanly with weatherproofing wrap
Measurement scale (ruler/tape measure) visible confirming calculated resonant element lengths
Written or verbal caption explaining the target frequency (e.g. 145 MHz VHF or 868 MHz LoRa) and calculated quarter-wavelength
Photo clearly displays the fully assembled field setup with handwritten student callsign/ID and date visible

lessons.outline:
1. The radio horizon equation: Calculating line-of-sight distance (D = 3.57 * (sqrt(h1) + sqrt(h2)))
2. Improvised antenna masts: Cured bamboo vs galvanized steel electrical conduit (EMT)
3. The 3-way guy wire geometry: 120-degree radial triangulation with earth screw anchors
4. Coaxial cable attenuation: RG-58 vs RG-213 vs LMR-400 (decibel signal loss per 10 meters)
5. The RF Choke (Ugly Balun): Coiling coaxial cable to suppress common-mode outer-shield currents
6. Lightning physics: Step potential, side-flashing, and induced electromagnetic pulse (EMP)
7. Single-point grounding: Coaxial gas discharge arrestors, 16 mm² copper wire, and 2.4m earth rods
8. PHOTO_CAPTURE practical: Construct and document an antenna build or RF grounding installation
